newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong, Macau impose checks after cyanide spill.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong, Macau impose checks after cyanide spill.

text.p: Macau banned people from bringing food in from China on Thursday and Hong Kong launched checks after a cyanide spillage into a south China river caused alarm throughtout the Pearl River delta region.
But the Chinese city where a truck carrying 200 drums of cyanide plunged into a tributary of the Pearl River, resumed drawing water from the river, Hong Kong government radio said.
Macau customs said residents of the Portugese-administered territory along the south China coast would not be allowed to bring in vegetables from China for private consumption.

Previously, Macau residents had been allowed to bring in small amounts of undeclared vegetables from Zhuhai city, just across the border, where food is much cheaper. Many locals go almost daily to the southern Chinese city to buy provisions.
A Macau customs spokesman said commerical imports would not be affected, but they would be inspected.

Action was also taken in Hong Kong. "As a precaution, we will take samples of produce from the mainland, especially vegetables and seafood, to check whether they are poisoned with cyanide," a Health Department spokeswoman told Reuters.

However, she said the risk was very slight, as most of the produce coming from China was from the area of Shenzhen, just across the border from the British colony and on the eastern side of the Pearl River delta.
Both Hong Kong and Macau, with scarce land resources, rely on imported food, mostly from China.
Health checks on food imports are routinely carried out, for example to guard against pesticide poisoning, but the cyanide checks are new to Hong Kong.
Authorities in southern China and Macau issued warnings on Wednesday of cyanide poisoning in waters there, but on Thursday they said they had resumed drawing water from the river.

An official from Wuzhou in Guangxi province was quoted on Hong Kong radio as saying that now only one of the 200 drums was missing and might have entered the West River. Earlier reports said three of the 200 drums were missing.
The official said the river water was found to contain only a small amount of the poison, well within the safety limits.
The chemical was intended use in for electroplating.
The river is a tributary of the Pearl River, which flows through heavily populated Guangdong province and into the South China Sea near Hong Kong and Macau.
Sales of bottled water in Macau have risen since the cyanide spill on Tuesday night. A cashier at a supermarket there said on Thursday that sales were "more than double the usual volume".
The territory's water company said it had suspended water imports from China, and that local water reserves were safe.
A spokeswoman from Hong Kong's water department said water supply was not in danger as water imported from China was from another tributary of the Pearl River system.

A Macau reporter returning from the Pearl River Delta region said that while the Chinese authorities appeared to have taken the cyanide spill seriously, the rural population seemed oblivious to any need for precautions.
"I saw women in a village washing clothes in a tributary of the West River," said Maria Cheang.
"Many people in the countryside are still fishing because they think if the fish are still alive then the water must still be okay," she said.
No deaths or sicknesses related to the spill have so far been reported in China, Macau or Hong Kong.
